# The Shortest-Path Algorithm Family

Four algorithms, one problem, four different sets of assumptions. SentinelNet in
[[discrete-mathematics-laboratories]] implements all four against the same graph, which is the only
way the trade-offs stop being a table to memorise — an instance of
[[multiple-solutions-side-by-side]].

| Algorithm | Scope | Complexity | Requires | Gives you |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Dijkstra** | single source | `O((V+E) log V)` with a heap | non-negative weights | the default |
| **Bellman–Ford** | single source | `O(V·E)` | nothing | negative weights **and negative-cycle detection** |
| **A\*** | single pair | Dijkstra-bounded | an admissible heuristic | far fewer expansions when geometry is known |
| **Floyd–Warshall** | all pairs | `O(V³)` | nothing | the full distance matrix, and transitive closure for free |

The choices that matter in practice:

- **Bellman–Ford is not a slower Dijkstra.** Its extra pass exists to *detect* negative cycles — a
  distance that keeps improving after `V−1` relaxations means no shortest path exists. Dijkstra
  cannot express that question.
- **A\* is Dijkstra plus a lower bound.** SentinelNet uses the **Haversine** great-circle distance as
  the heuristic. It is admissible because straight-line distance over the sphere can never exceed
  travel along edges, and admissibility is precisely what preserves optimality.
- **Floyd–Warshall wins when you need every pair.** Running Dijkstra `V` times is asymptotically
  better on sparse graphs but loses on dense ones and costs far more code.

SentinelNet backs Dijkstra with a **hand-written binary MinHeap** rather than a library priority
queue, which is the difference between `O((V+E) log V)` and the naive `O(V²)`.

Q-HYDRO, at 25 nodes, deliberately does not bother, and says why:

> "Note: Prim and Dijkstra use simple `O(V·E)` / `O(V²)` implementations for readability. At
> `|V| = 25` this is instant; swap in a binary heap for scale."
> — Discrete-Mathematics-Laboratories/lab5_GraphTheory/Q-HYDRO Wrocław/README.md, 2026-06-09

Two implementations of the same algorithm in one repo under opposite priorities, each stating its
reason — see [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]].

## The TSP tail — and a correction

Beyond shortest paths, SentinelNet attempts tours: **nearest-neighbour** construction, **2-opt**
improvement, and a function named `tspChristofides`.

**That function is not Christofides.** Christofides guarantees a tour within 1.5× optimal by taking a
minimum spanning tree, finding a **minimum-weight perfect matching** on the odd-degree vertices,
combining them into an Eulerian multigraph and short-cutting the Euler tour. `sn-algo.js` matches the
odd-degree vertices **greedily**. Greedy matching can be arbitrarily worse than optimal, so the
1.5-approximation bound is lost — what remains is a *Christofides-shaped heuristic* with no proven
ratio. `confidence: high`, read directly from source. It should not be cited as Christofides.
